Continued - THE STRONG MEN WE ARE RAISING

Yesterday’s post sparked quite a few reactions.

And I think one thing needs to be made clear:

This is not an argument against change.

It was never about saying the younger generation is doomed.

If anything, it was meant to make us look beyond the trend, understand the psychology behind it, and question the kind of future we are collectively building.

Let me take it a step further.

I remember being on another space where people were projecting what the next generation would become.

Some said they were genuinely scared.

That the next generation would be worse.
Less disciplined.
Less responsible.
Less connected to reality.
But I remember thinking:

Haven’t people said the same thing about every generation?

I vividly remember my parents talking about their generation with a certain dignity and telling us how different and sometimes disappointing they feared ours would become.

Yet look at what our generation has produced.

Nigeria has produced people who have built companies, technologies and institutions that operate far beyond our borders:

Shola Akinlade & Ezra Olubi built Paystack, which Stripe acquired for more than $200 million.

Iyinoluwa Aboyeji co-founded Andela and Flutterwave and has continued investing in Africa’s next generation of founders.

Olugbenga “GB” Agboola helped build Flutterwave into one of Africa’s most significant payment companies.

Odunayo Eweniyi, alongside her PiggyVest co-founders, helped build one of Nigeria’s most influential savings and investment platforms.

And this isn’t limited to fintech.
We have Nigerian engineers, creators, designers, founders, artists, researchers and builders solving problems that previous generations couldn’t even imagine.

We have young Nigerians building in:

AI
Blockchain
Fintech
Software
Media
Entertainment
Fashion
Education
Creative technology

And even among the younger generation, there are already people proving that the story isn’t simply one of decline.
There are young developers teaching other teenagers to code, young entrepreneurs building businesses, and young Nigerians creating communities around technology and innovation.

So yes, I agree with the “OLODO uprising.”

But I also believe in something else:

THE GENIUS UPRISING.

The builders.

The thinkers.

The disciplined.

The curious.

The ones who understand that going viral is not the same thing as building value.

The ones who understand that money is not the same thing as wealth.

The ones who understand that freedom without responsibility is not progress.

And this is where the conversation becomes personal.

Because the real question isn’t:

“What is wrong with Gen Z?”

The real question is:

“What kind of next generation are YOU raising?”

Because somewhere in the future, your children will become someone else’s leaders.

They will become:

Founders.
Engineers.
Doctors.
Investors.
Policymakers.
Teachers.
Creators.
Parents.
Builders.

And I want to raise children who can look at the world they inherited and say:

“Our parents didn’t fail us.”

I want to raise children who are evidence that despite everything happening around us, we still understood the assignment.

Children who can embrace technology without becoming slaves to it.

Children who can enjoy freedom without abandoning responsibility.

Children who can understand modernity without despising their heritage.

Children who can pursue wealth without losing their values.

Children who can be ambitious without becoming entitled.

Children who can question the world without losing the ability to think.

Because the future isn’t automatically going to be better.

We have to build the people capable of making it better.

And that brings us back to the cycle:

Hard times create strong men. Strong men create good times. Good times create weak men. And weak men create hard times.

Yesterday, I was talking about the cycle.

Today, I’m asking you to look in the mirror.

Are you raising the generation that will break the cycle or continue it?

Because perhaps the future isn’t determined by what Gen Z becomes.

Perhaps it is determined by what we choose to raise.
And that is a much more personal question.

@Teknium I ran out of OpenAI resets building Hermes with Hermes this week.

So I built Freemaxxing.

That is not a joke. Developers are already spending an absolutely stupid amount of money on tokens. When you’re building with agents all day, eventually you hit a quota, a rate limit, a weekly cap, or the point where you simply refuse to put another $100 into the token furnace.

And the difference between “I’m done working for today” and “keep going” can literally just be having a free model available.

So I made that a first-class Hermes primitive!

Freemaxxing is a bundled Hermes model provider backed by a local OpenAI-compatible proxy. Hermes talks to it like any other provider. Behind that interface, it builds a pool of whatever usable inference you already have available:

Tier 0: Nous Portal. It automatically discovers the OAuth/JWT credentials Hermes already has. No new API key. No new account setup. The JWT can rotate, so Freemaxxing re-resolves it on expiry instead of dying halfway through a long-running gateway.

Tier 1: OpenRouter. Optional. If you already have an OPENROUTER_API_KEY, it joins the pool.

Tier 2: Hugging Face. Optional. Same thing with HF_TOKEN.

Then the fun part starts.

Freemaxxing queries each backend’s /models catalog and does model-aware routing. If you ask for a specific model, it prefers a backend that actually advertises it.

Or just ask for the virtual model:

freemaxxing

That means auto.

The router looks at the live catalogs, prefers :free models first, then lighter flash / mini / nano / small / lite models, and sends the request to an available backend.

And it actually behaves like a pool rather than a dumb proxy:

429? Honor Retry-After, cool that backend down, try another.

5xx, timeout, connection reset? Cooldown and fail over.

404 because that backend doesn’t have the model? Skip it without poisoning the backend.

Expired Nous credential? Refresh the JWT and retry.

Bad request? Fail immediately instead of spraying the same malformed request across every provider.

Streaming? Passed straight through.

Tools, response_format, seed, stop sequences, top_p, and the rest of the OpenAI request body? Preserved.

Everything dead? 503. It does not secretly reach for some expensive provider behind your back.

There’s even /healthz exposing the state of the pool.

And I didn’t want this implemented as another special case welded into Hermes forever, so I widened the provider architecture itself. ProviderProfile now has a generic supports_noauth_loopback capability. Any future plugin can declare itself a local no-key provider and participate normally in Hermes provider discovery, credential resolution, model selection, fallbacks, and the provider catalog.

The proxy is also dormant unless you actually select Freemaxxing. Merely discovering the plugin doesn’t start a listener or grab a port.

So yeah.

I exhausted my paid AI allowance.

Instead of stopping work, I changed Hermes so running out of paid tokens no longer has to mean running out of AI.

That is Freemaxxing. 😈

And of course the PR is green.

HON. NOAH AHMED — EMPOWERING THE GEN Z GENERATION

Hon. Noah Ahmed’s proposed vision for young people is built on one fundamental principle: young people should not only be the leaders of tomorrow—they should have meaningful opportunities to contribute today.

His youth empowerment agenda would focus on turning the energy, creativity and innovation of Gen Z into skills, businesses, employment and sustainable livelihoods across Taraba State.

Under this proposed vision, youth development would include:

💡 TECHNOLOGY & DIGITAL SKILLS
Create opportunities for young people to learn AI, cybersecurity, software development, digital marketing, graphics, content creation and other emerging technologies.

🚀 STARTUP & BUSINESS SPONSORSHIP
Support promising youth-owned businesses through transparent grants, equipment, mentorship and access to business development programmes—not just one-time handouts.

🎓 EDUCATION & SCHOLARSHIPS
Expand opportunities for scholarships, vocational training, professional certifications and technical education so that financial hardship does not prevent talented young people from developing their potential.

🎨 CREATIVE INDUSTRY SUPPORT
Provide structured support for musicians, filmmakers, photographers, designers, writers, fashion entrepreneurs and other creatives through training, sponsorship and platforms for showcasing their work.

⚽ SPORTS DEVELOPMENT
Invest in grassroots sports by supporting young athletes, coaches and sporting programmes, while creating pathways for talented youths to compete at higher levels.

💼 JOBS, INTERNSHIPS & ENTREPRENEURSHIP
Build partnerships with private businesses and institutions to create internships, apprenticeships and employment opportunities while helping young entrepreneurs develop sustainable enterprises.

🏢 YOUTH INNOVATION CENTRES
Develop spaces where young people can access training, internet connectivity, mentorship, technology and collaborative opportunities.

A NEW APPROACH TO YOUTH SPONSORSHIP

The goal should be to move from “giving young people something” to “giving young people the tools to build something.”

Every sponsorship programme should be transparent, merit-based and accessible to young people across communities and local government areas.

HON. NOAH AHMED’S MESSAGE TO THE GEN Z GENERATION:

> “Your ideas matter. Your talent matters. Your future matters. Government should create an environment where a young person with an idea, skill or dream has a genuine opportunity to turn that potential into reality.”

Empower the youth. Invest in talent. Sponsor innovation. Create opportunity. Build a stronger Taraba.

AI IS CHANGING FASHION, AND IT’S BIGGER THAN IMAGE GENERATION.🧵

Artificial Intelligence is quietly transforming almost every stage of the fashion value chain.

From design and trend forecasting to marketing, production, e-commerce, and customer experience, AI is changing how fashion businesses operate.

🧵Here are a few areas where the impact is already visible:

🔹 Design & Ideation:- Exploring silhouettes, patterns, colors, and collection concepts faster.

🔹 Trend Forecasting:-  Using data to identify emerging consumer preferences and market trends.

🔹 Virtual Prototyping:-  Visualizing designs before spending heavily on materials and production.

🔹 Personalization:- Helping brands recommend products and experiences based on customer preferences.

🔹 Marketing & Content:-  Accelerating campaign concepts, storytelling, product descriptions, and visual development.

🔹 Demand Forecasting:- Helping brands make smarter production and inventory decisions, potentially reducing waste.

But here’s what I find most interesting:

AI may not replace the fashion designer. It may replace some of the limitations that slow the designer down.

Creativity still requires taste.

Culture still requires understanding.

Craftsmanship still requires skill.

And strategy still requires human judgment.

For African fashion, this presents an even bigger opportunity.

Imagine combining African heritage, traditional craftsmanship, modern design thinking, and AI-powered innovation to build globally competitive fashion brands.

The question is no longer:

“Will AI affect fashion?”

It already is.

The better question is:

👉🏼How will fashion entrepreneurs use AI to build better brands, products, and businesses?”

This Paper is one of the cleverest solutions I’ve seen for fixing Diffusion Alignment.

If you’ve worked with RLHF or Reward Backprop on DiTs, you must be tired of delayed feedback. 

Evaluating only the final image makes credit assignment a total nightmare. 

You either run out of VRAM trying to unroll the full trajectory, or you fight insane gradient variance with online RL.

The authors solve this by sticking learnable, position-free "register tokens" into a frozen DiT. 

Instead of waiting until step 50, these registers pull dense reward signals directly out of noisy intermediate latents. 

It turns out you can accurately judge trajectory quality surprisingly early in the denoising process.

What makes this paper stand out is how practical the applications are:

1-For training: Their distillation setup (RG-OPD) skips standard policy gradients entirely and hits the same alignment performance while using up to 33x fewer GPU hours. That’s huge for making alignment accessible.

2-For inference: You can use their Reward-Guided Sampling (RGS) to steer generation live off these register gradients thus improving both prompt adherence and visual quality without retraining or touching model weights.

It’s a super clean, well thought-out approach that addresses both the compute bottleneck and inference control at once. 

Definitely worth a read if you're working on generative models:

GPT IMAGE 2 + MIINIMAX H3 WITH PROMPTS

What if your AI tools became a cinematic universe? 

I wanted to try something a little different with MiniMax H3 and create a commercial for LOVART AI that feels more like a fashion campaign than a typical tech ad.

I put my virtual influencer, Alexa Grey, in LOVART’s bright yellow and white colors and built the whole concept around text, characters and visual storytelling.

One thing I really wanted to explore was how far I could push the typography.

MiniMax prompts use editorial typography, characters crossing through letters, billboards, graphic cards, oversized text, parallax and visual transitions.

So instead of simply putting a model name on screen, I made the lettering part of the world.

Alexa walks through giant words.
Characters move around the typography.
Billboards become cinematic scenes.
Letters transform into environments.
Graphic cards transition into completely different worlds.

And then I brought the AI models into the story:

The goal was to make everything feel connected — characters, typography, billboards, environments and AI models all living inside the same creative universe.

And at the end, it all comes together as: 
LOVART AI: YOUR AI CREATIVE STUDIO.

No dialogue. No voiceover.

Just visuals, music, typography, and motion.
